Wordmark treatments · round four

The mark as a lit material

Can a generated image give the wordmark more attitude — without the generator ever seeing a letterform? Yes: it supplies the material and the light, never the shape. Two of the round's findings are corrections to its own first answers.

The band has now seen this work. Reported 2026‑08‑30: every member read the shared material and looked at the artwork. They like the wordmark, the skull, the year rings and the timeline, and they love the illustrated generated work.

That is a response to a direction, not a signature on each item. Individual artefacts, whether Böbbis becomes a standing per-release character, whether the skull is ever publicly named, and printing or selling anything are all still open. Where a direction was chosen inside a round, that was Marcus’s call.

Start with the plain-language overview if you haven’t already.

That review predates this round. The band read the shared material on 2026‑08‑30. Round four was made on 2026‑08‑31 and nobody outside this session has seen it — not the band, and not Marcus at the time of writing. Nothing in it has been chosen, and nothing in it changes the wordmark they did see.

00

Where this sits

This is the fourth round of wordmark surface treatments. Rounds one and two drew 26 of them; round three asked a generator to make them and every one of its ten candidates came back a different word. This round asks a third question: can a generated image contribute to the mark without the generator ever seeing a letterform?

These are explorations, not proposals. Nothing here is written to assets/, nothing amends the shipped mark, and — as in rounds one to three — USAGE.md's no-effects rule is broken on purpose. The wordmark the band actually uses is unchanged and is not in question.

The question, from Marcus, 2026-08-30: “Can we generate texture for the wordmark and use it to make the wordmark have even more attitude than just an illustration based treatment as we do today? Can we for example create a metal texture and use the wordmark as a mask, and do another darker texture and create a ‘3d’ mask from the wordmark, so by combining the two create a 3d metal wordmark. Or is there an even better way?”

The answer is yes, and it is the first safe way this project has found to put a generated image on the mark. The model is handed a rectangle and asked for material, or a sphere and asked for light. It is never shown a letterform, so the geometry stays the shipped master exactly — the same property that makes any scripted treatment safe: a script repaints a path, it never redraws the word.

That safety lives in the mask, not in the module. Hand a generated wordmark to this code and it is a generated wordmark, with all of round three's problems. The separation gate used here measures contrast and enclosure — it cannot see whether the letterforms are still Apezone. A beautifully legible wrong word passes it.

01

The hypothesis was right; its second half aimed at the wrong target

Marcus's construction had two textures: metal through the mark as a mask, plus a darker one through an offset “3D mask”. The first half is sound. The second half describes a treatment this project already has, with photographs substituted for flat colour, and it fails twice.

An offset bevels in one direction only. The existing depth treatments build their edge by subtracting the shape from its own translated copy, so they light the top-left of every stroke and shade the bottom-right — and get the O's counter backwards, because the inside of a hole slopes the other way. At cartoon scale with flat colour that reads as a convention. Under a photographic material it reads as a mistake.

A photograph of metal has its lighting already in it. Pasted flat through a mask, its highlights sit where the photographer's window was, not where this letterform turns. That is the glued on complaint the illustration register already traced to its cause, arriving by a new route.

So the work is split three ways, each source doing the one thing it is good at: the generated plate gives micro-structure and nothing else — it is high-passed, and its colour and its own lighting are discarded; the environment gives the lighting; and the picture gives the colour, as decision 18 requires. Generated material never carries colour into the mark.

02

The generated plates: a real but small gain, and one clean failure

As a shader the plate works, and it is modest. Visibly cast, pitted metal at full strength. But the separation gate barely moves for it — 1.97 to 2.03. The plate changes the surface, not the mark's hold on the artwork underneath.

The cracked paint failed as a shader, and the failure is structural rather than a tuning problem. Flaking paint is discontinuous: a flake is present or it is gone. Perturbing a surface normal can only bend a continuous surface, so it came out as mottling.

03

That failure located the second texture's real job

Marcus's second texture does have a job. It is not on the face — it is in the mask. Biting the plate's structure out of the ink reads as corroded metal, and it is the strongest drawn result in the round.

It moves the silhouette, which nothing else in the module does. That is the same class of change as the round-two treatment that put spurs on the terminals, and it is labelled the same way. The cost is measurable against the gate this project already calibrated for “is it still the wordmark”:

bite0.100.200.250.300.350.45
IoU vs master0.9700.9370.9230.9070.8890.857

The calibrated pass mark is 0.90. The version that reads best sits at 0.889 — below the line. A bite of 0.28 (IoU 0.91) is the most damage available inside it.

The IoU cost is plate-independent by construction. The erosion removes a percentile of erodible ink, so the fraction removed — and therefore the IoU — is set by the amount asked for and by nothing else. The forged and cracked-paint columns come out near-identical because the measure was built that way, not because the two materials are interchangeable. The plate chooses the damage's shape; it never chooses its amount.

An earlier version thresholded the plate's absolute value instead and removed 0.3% while being asked for 55%.

04

The reference, and the thing every treatment was missing

On 2026-08-31 Marcus posted a blackletter chrome wordmark: “this was kinda what I was aiming for.” Then, fairly: “This image I pasted is I guess fully generated. So it can be difficult to replicate the way you do it.”

He is right about the difficulty. He is also pointing at the reason the picture cannot simply be generated for us: in that image the letterforms are whatever the model drew, and nobody has to check them. Ours has a corrected O, a kerning pass and a 7.43:1 ratio on record. Three of the reference's properties were describable, and one of them was the whole gap.

No plateau. Every stroke there is a roof: the height rises from both edges and meets at a ridge, so the surface is turning everywhere and the environment is swept across the full width of every stroke. That is why one stroke runs from near-black to white. A fixed bevel structurally cannot do it — it rises, then flattens, and a flat face has one normal.

Neutral silver, and no keyline. Silver is not a departure from the palette: Ink, Steel, Bone and Paper are a chrome ramp. It does spend the per-poster accent, which is a real trade rather than a free win.

Star glints. The first attempt blurred the whole bright mask, which on a roofed stroke is a long ridge line — so it smeared rectangles across the word and read as digital tearing. A flare comes off a point: a handful of genuine local maxima, thinned so two never overlap, each drawn as a cross with an exponential falloff.

The ridge normalisation is global, and it is only sound because this master is near-monoline. A face with modulated strokes would have its thin parts roof early and its thick parts never reach the ridge. That case needs a medial-axis normalisation, which this is not.

05

Generating the light instead of the material — and it failed first

A matcap is a photograph of a sphere, and a sphere carries an entire lighting environment in one image, already reflected. So the model can supply the light while the master supplies the geometry and the picture supplies the colour — and the model still never sees a letterform.

Used raw, all five variants failed the separation gate on the dark source and passed on the bright one — the exact inverse of the procedural environment. The cause is measurable rather than aesthetic: a real chrome ball in a dark studio is mostly reflecting darkness.

median over the discmean5th pct95th pct
generated matcap, raw0.0750.2560.0120.969
procedural environment0.4230.4620.0001.000

A 5.6× gap in the middle of the range. Every mark it shaded came out dark, and a dark mark on a night picture has nothing to separate with.

A photograph's absolute level belongs to the studio it was shot in, not to the design it is being used for. The disc is stretched to its own 1st–99th percentiles and then gamma-corrected until its median lands where a design ramp expects it, with the exponent solved rather than dialled. Structure — the whole reason to generate a sphere — survives; only the level becomes ours.

After that correction the two best variants pass both sources: 4.98 and 5.48 on the dark picture, 1.93 and 1.96 on the bright one.

A claim made during the round did not survive it. Before the defect in §06 was fixed, the hand-written chrome failed the bright picture at 1.21, and the generated environment was reported as more robust. Fixing that defect moved the hand-written version to passing both, so the comparison no longer holds. What the final numbers support is narrower: the generated sphere holds a wider margin on the bright picture and sits marginally lower on the dark one. And being generated is not itself robustness — the second sphere fails the bright picture. One of the two.

The frame instruction was not obeyed, and it mattered. Both spheres came back centred on white with a margin rather than tangent to the frame. A fixed centre crop would have sampled paper at the rim and hung a bright halo on every stroke, so the loader locates the disc instead of trusting the framing. Any future plate goes through it.

06

One defect that only appeared at the end

The distance transform returns whole-pixel distances, so the height field is a staircase. Across a narrow bevel that is invisible. A roof spans the whole stroke and its gradient is what gets sampled, so against the generated sphere's smooth gradients the steps showed up as contour terracing down every diagonal. Smoothing now scales with the span.

Worth recording because of when it appeared: the defect existed from the moment the roof profile was introduced, and was invisible until the environment got good enough to expose it. A gentle procedural ramp was hiding it.

07

Method, budget and limits

600 credits of 5 900 available: 400 on four material plates, 200 on two chrome spheres. Balance 5 900 → 5 300. Every other environment in the round is procedural, so the mechanism was proved at zero cost before anything was bought. All six generations went through the project's one route, at the model seedream-5-pro; both prompts are recorded verbatim in plates/PROMPTS.md.

Every candidate was measured at the size and position a poster actually puts the mark, on two real sources chosen to be opposites — one dark, one bright — with the eight shipped treatments carried alongside as controls.

What this cannot show:

  • Nothing here has been printed. Every judgement is a screen judgement.
  • Two artworks is not a corpus. The controls are a sanity check, not a survey.
  • Nothing measures “attitude”. The gate answers does it separate. Whether any of this beats the drawn treatments is a judgement nobody has made yet.
  • The marks were checked at full-size crop, not at poster viewing distance.
  • The erosion figure is a statement about pixels, not about recognition.
  • The separation gate cannot see letterform identity. Only the mask makes that impossible here.
08

Open, and needing Marcus

  1. Is any of this better than the drawn treatments? Not answered. The gate vetoes; it does not choose, and nobody has chosen.
  2. Erosion below the IoU line. The 0.90 mark was calibrated against generated candidates, where nobody knew what had changed. Here we know exactly what changed and by how much. Whether that justifies letting it go is a decision, not a measurement.
  3. Neutral chrome spends the per-poster accent that decision 18 asks for. The half-tinted version is the compromise; nobody has said whether the trade is acceptable.
  4. Library or exploration? It plugs into the poster builder today as a callable, without modifying it.
  5. Print and merchandise licence untouched. The three gates in notes/merch-licence.md apply to every plate and sphere here exactly as to any other generated image.

Round four of the wordmark surface-treatment rounds. Rounds one and two are wordmark-fun.html and wordmark-bold.html; round three, the generated one, is wordmark-magnific.html. The shipped wordmark is unchanged by all four.
